clinicalPearls: The commonest form of cutaneous mastocytosis, presenting as multiple red-brown macules and papules
Lesions urticate on rubbing (Darier sign) and may blister in young children
It can begin in infancy or in adulthood, with different implications for each
Childhood-onset disease often regresses spontaneously, while adult-onset disease is frequently associated with systemic mastocytosis
Mediator release can cause flushing, itch and, uncommonly, systemic reactions
Baseline serum tryptase and clinical assessment guide the need for systemic evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: Urticaria pigmentosa is a maculopapular pattern of cutaneous mastocytosis in which increased numbers of clonal mast cells accumulate in the dermis, commonly linked to KIT mutations. Mechanical or chemical stimulation degranulates these mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators to produce the localised weal-and-flare of the Darier sign and the pigmented appearance from associated increased melanin. As with other cutaneous mastocytosis, childhood disease tends to involute, whereas adult disease often reflects an underlying systemic process.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of cutaneous or systemic mastocytosis
Secondary syphilis or other papular eruptions
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing increased dermal mast cells if needed
Assessment for systemic symptoms and, in adults, systemic mastocytosis
redFlags: Extensive disease with blistering in infants
reference.prognosis: Childhood urticaria pigmentosa commonly improves or clears by adolescence, whereas adult disease tends to persist and may be a marker of systemic mastocytosis.
pitfalls: Failing to evaluate adults for systemic mastocytosis
Provoking mediator release by vigorously rubbing lesions
